extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in the history, forms, and genres of the novel (including creative-writing students)
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic survey of the novel as a literary form: its historical development, major movements (romanticism, realism, modernism, postmodernism), genre conventions, and non-traditional formats in the 20th–21st centuries. Useful as background for writers, students, and scholars considering form, technique, and market contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel as a middle-class genre / focus on ordinary life
rubrics_metrics.description: Ian Watt: the novel developed in the social context of the rise of the Middle Class; 'Robinson Crusoe is certainly the first novel in the sense that it is the first fictional narrative in which an ordinary person's daily activities are the center of continuous literary attention.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of quotidian, middle-class perspectives and attention to everyday activities is a defining characteristic in Watt's account of the novel. This is a historical/critical criterion for identifying early modern novels; debates exist about whether Robinson Crusoe is 'the first novel.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Gothic / Romantic novel characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Romanticism and the revived romance genre (e.g., gothic fiction) challenged realism: Gothic romances 'exploited the grotesque' and were accused of exploiting topics to 'thrill, arouse, or horrify' audiences; romantic novelists argued they were 'exploring the entire realm of fictionality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect emphasis on marvelous/uncommon incidents, the grotesque, psychological depths (sexuality, anxieties, desires). Examples: The Castle of Otranto; The Mysteries of Udolpho; works by Poe, Mary Shelley, E.T.A. Hoffmann, and de Sade. Useful as a checklist for tone, subject-matter, and the acceptance of sensational or transgressive content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical novel: combine documentary research with imaginative re-evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Walter Scott's 'true historical novel' used historical research and documentary sources but re-evaluated history through imagination, rendering incidents and protagonists in ways only the novelist could do and combining research with 'marvelous and uncommon incidents.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A historical novel should show grounding in research and documentary material while using imaginative techniques to make the past emotionally and narratively vivid. Scott's method is presented as a model: balance factual grounding with creative interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stream-of-consciousness / interior monologue technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Modernists replaced the 18th- and 19th-century narrator with texts that attempted to record inner thoughts — a 'stream of consciousness' — and used 'interior monologue.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique emphasizes direct presentation of characters' mental life rather than mediated narration. Cited practitioners: James Joyce (Ulysses), Dorothy Richardson, Marcel Proust, Virginia Woolf, William Faulkner; term first used by William James (1890). Consider use for interiority, subjectivity, and experimental narrative voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modernist / experimental fragmentation and non-linearity
rubrics_metrics.description: Some 20th-century authors fragmented their stories and challenged time and sequentiality (e.g., Robert Coover), and expressionist works interspersed non-fictional text fragments alongside fiction to create alternative forms of realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accepts disrupted chronology, montage, and textual fragmentation as deliberate formal choices. Examples: Alfred Döblin (Berlin Alexanderplatz), Samuel Beckett (Molloy, Malone Dies, The Unnamable), Julio Cortázar (Rayuela), Thomas Pynchon. Use when aiming to break conventional narrative structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postmodern techniques: intertextuality and metafiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Postmodern authors subverted claims of originality by playing with existing materials, treating language as self-referential, and making wide use of intertextual references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect metafictional play, explicit referencing of other texts, and skepticism about originality. Examples: Thomas Pynchon, Umberto Eco (The Name of the Rose, Foucault's Pendulum). Useful as criteria for assessing postmodern works' self-consciousness and intertextual complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre fiction: declare genre and meet reader expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular fiction production employs direct, short-term marketing strategies by openly declaring a work's genre; popular novels are based entirely on expectations for that genre and often create series with an identifiable brand name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For commercial/genre-oriented writing, adherence to genre conventions and clear branding (series format, recurring characters) is a deliberate strategy. Example: Sherlock Holmes series. Measure success by how well a work satisfies its genre's conventional expectations and its target readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular fiction marketing and controversial topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors of popular fiction tend to advertise that they have exploited a controversial topic; because they serve fan communities they can risk offending literary critics (e.g., Dan Brown discussing Da Vinci Code).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial authors may prioritize reader engagement and controversy over critical approbation. Consider marketing posture and audience response as part of evaluating such works; blurring between 'popular' and 'serious' literature is noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Romance / love-romance lineage and market significance
rubrics_metrics.description: The twentieth-century love romance descends from early-modern romance writers; romance fiction holds a substantial market share (estimated $1.375 billion in the US book market in 2007).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing or evaluating romance, consider both traditions (literary lineage) and market dynamics; commercial viability and formulaic expectations are part of the genre's evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphic novel: comic-strip format published as a book
rubrics_metrics.description: A graphic novel is 'a fictional story that is presented in comic-strip format and published as a book' (though the term can also refer to non-fiction and collections of short works).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format-focused criterion: visual storytelling, panel composition, and book-form presentation are central. Note manga as a major national tradition and that the form can encompass non-fiction or anthologies; evaluate both visual and verbal storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-traditional/digital formats: ebooks, web fiction, and web serials
rubrics_metrics.description: A major 21st-century development: novels published as ebooks and the growth of web fiction; a common type is the web serial, where novels are frequently published in parts over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Digital formats favor serialized release, ongoing reader engagement, and often enable self-publishing. Examples and market notes: Joara (S. Korea) with large numbers of writers and serials; web fiction is highly commercial in some markets (China, South Korea). Evaluate pacing, serialization strategy, and platform/monetization implications for craft and career.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audiobooks as a format
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiobooks are recordings of a book reading; they have been available since the 1930s and became more widely available and online in recent decades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production values (narration, sound design) matter to the form; consider the performative dimension when adapting prose to audio. Audiobook availability affects reach and accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novels as vehicles for social and political issues (social responsibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: From the 19th century onward, novels began to deal with difficult subjects—current political and social issues—making 'social responsibility' a key subject for authors. Debates focused on the moral soundness of the modern novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works aiming to engage social/political topics are often assessed on their fidelity to social reality, persuasive power, and ethical implications. Examples: Dickens, Hardy, Émile Zola, Uncle Tom's Cabin; consider how narrative viewpoint and evidentiary detail influence social critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science fiction and fantasy reflect technological and social contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Science fiction and fantasy have developed in response to industrialization, Darwin's theory, Marxism, technological change, and other social forces; such works often explore interactions between humans and machines, post-apocalyptic scenarios, and virtual realities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate speculative works by their engagement with contemporary scientific, technological, or social ideas and how plausibly and imaginatively they extrapolate consequences. Examples: Jules Verne, H. G. Wells, Ursula K. Le Guin, William Gibson.
